description: Two-person team at the Kuching hub tackling Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. Ashley: CS student (web dev, UI, video editing). Johnson: Mechanical Engineering (EVA limits, walking-cost models). We’re building Marswalk Planner: plan a route across Jezero Crater using layered NASA data (terrain, slope, radiation), then walk it in first-person 3D with a sci-fi HUD. Looking for: Three.js/3D, geospatial data (Python, GDAL, DEM), planetary science, UI design. Beginners welcome!
summary: Marswalk Planner is a browser-based 3D game that turns the USGS geologic map of Jezero Crater into a walkable survival guide. Players explore the crater as an astronaut, where every surface matches a real mapped geologic unit — delta deposits, crater floor, dunes, and rim. They plan their own routes under real constraints: limited oxygen and suit battery, radiation exposure, darkness at night, and sudden dust storms. Along the way, they collect rock and soil samples with tweezers and a trowel, photograph discoveries, and keep a field journal. To survive, they must return to a lander inspired by NASA’s CobraMRV concept, entering through a rear-entry suitport to refill oxygen, recharge, plan routes at the mission table, and shelter from radiation. A true Martian clock — 24 h 39 min sols, a 687-day year, a seasonal sun path and a 25% yearly chance of a global dust storm — shows when it is safe to go out and how far you can go. It runs in any desktop browser with no installation.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Marswalk Planner is a first-person Mars survival game set in Jezero Crater, built for the browser with HTML and Three.js. The player is an astronaut who sets out from their lander. They walk across real Martian terrain, collect samples at science sites, and must get back safely before oxygen, battery or daylight run out.

  • Real terrain: Jezero Crater and the Nili Planum plateau are rebuilt 1:1 from NASA/USGS’s Geologic Map of Jezero Crater and the Nili Planum Region, Mars (Sun & Stack, 2020, 1:75,000) — about 64 × 67 km of delta fans, Neretva Vallis, the crater rim, etched plateaus, dunes and impact craters. Each mapped unit has its own relief, surface texture and rock density. Rock and soil textures come from Perseverance rover images. Players can find 14 science sites across the map.
  • Sample collection: Tweezers pick up gravel and loose pieces, and a trowel digs soil or breaks rocks. Samples are stored in a jar the player can inspect up close; each soil scoop forms its own coloured layer, with weights in grams. A logbook tracks which of the 14 sites are complete, and a camera saves discoveries to a photo album.
  • Route planning: Players choose their own routes, and footprints show the path they have walked. The geologic map shows where they are and can be used to jump between regions.
    • One sol lasts 24 h 39 min 35 s, and a year is 668.6 sols (687 Earth days).
    • The sun’s path follows Jezero’s latitude and the season.
    • Nights are dark, with stars and a blue Martian sunset, so a helmet torch with high and low beams is needed.
    • Each Mars year has a 25% chance of a dust storm that cuts visibility and sunlight.
  • The habitat: The astronaut climbs the ladder and docks into a rear-entry suitport, climbs out of the back of the suit into the airlock, then opens the inner hatch. Inside are a life-support panel to refill oxygen and recharge the suit, a mission table showing the geologic map for route planning, a workstation, and a radiation-shielded bunk to sleep until dawn or wait out a dust storm.
  • Views & HUD: First-person helmet view and third-person view. The helmet HUD shows mission time, oxygen, radiation, heart rate, outside temperature, weather, compass, battery and a map.
  • Intro & sound: A cinematic film of launch, cruise, entry and landing flows straight into gameplay. A Mars soundtrack plays in the background and is muffled when you are inside the habitat.

What benefits does it have?

  • Maps you can feel: It turns a static geologic map into a place you can walk through. Distance, slope and terrain type become something you experience, not just read.
  • Real trade-offs: Players learn the trade-offs of a real surface walk (EVA): how far they can go, when to turn back, and how night and dust storms change the plan.
  • Science context: Sampling across different geologic units connects gameplay to the science Perseverance does at Jezero.
  • Easy access: It runs in any desktop browser with no installation, so classrooms, outreach events and the public can play from a single link.

What is the intended impact?

On Mars, the shortest path is rarely the safest. Players must balance oxygen, battery, radiation, time of day and terrain while completing their science tasks. Through that, they learn why route planning, consumables and equipment design decide whether an astronaut survives. We hope it sparks curiosity about Mars exploration in students and the public, and gives an intuitive picture of what a crewed surface mission would demand.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Three.js (WebGL), with custom shaders for terrain, sky, rocks and lighting
  • Web Workers for terrain generation, Web Audio for music, and Media Source Extensions to stream the HD intro film
  • Blender and glTF for the rigged astronaut model
  • GitHub Pages for hosting
  • Audio: all music and sound sourced and edited by our team
    • Geologic Map of Jezero Crater and the Nili Planum Region, Mars (Sun & Stack, 2020; USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3464, 1:75,000), prepared for NASA’s Planetary Science Division and based on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX imagery — https://usgs.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=a0ae4b521f7a4a6ca2cf0f0c551d5293
    • NASA Perseverance rover imagery (rock and soil textures)
    • NASA CobraMRV lander concept (habitat design)
    • Mars physical constants: sol length, year length, axial tilt (time and season model)

How is your project creative?

  • The destination is never forced: players read the ground and choose their own routes, and footprints record their decisions.
  • A real Martian clock with seasons, nights and dust storms turns the map into a survival guide that changes over time.
  • The rear-entry suitport is playable: you back into the suit through the habitat wall and climb out of it into the airlock, showing how dust stays out of the cabin.
  • The intro film flows seamlessly into the game, linking the journey to Mars with the work on the surface.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Realism grounded in research: Before building, we read widely on crewed Mars missions and studied many real Mars photos and references, so the planet looks as close to reality as we could make it.
  • Landing & habitat: We compared ways to slow a crewed capsule for a safe Mars landing, including supersonic retropropulsion and aerodynamic braking. Through that research we found NASA’s CobraMRV concept, a vehicle that carries crew and cargo and becomes the living module after landing. We based both the exterior and the interior of our habitat on it.
  • Spacesuit: Apollo-style suits are too bulky for Mars fieldwork. Starting from NASA’s designs, we made a lighter suit with flexible joints so the astronaut can bend down to pick up samples. Rear entry lets the astronaut get in and out through the habitat wall without carrying toxic Martian dust into the cabin.
  • Playability: We kept realism where it teaches (sol length, seasons, consumables, the suitport) and simplified where it would slow play.
  • Accessibility: It is a browser-only build, so anyone with the link can play without installing anything.
  • Our work vs. AI: The concept, story, research, habitat and spacesuit design, gameplay design and every creative decision are our own. We also sourced and edited all the audio ourselves. AI (Claude) was used only as a production tool to generate the visuals, images and the code that renders them, following our designs and direction.
